1:
The heading puts this chapter earlier than the one before it, and the voices differ on what follows. Gill sets the sequence out, the preceding prophecy belonging to the fourth year and this to the accession, with Josiah lately dead and his son deposed after three months by the king of Egypt. Clarke calls it totally out of its place and reports two scholars who would move it, one before a much later chapter and one much earlier still. Ellicott dates it to the very earliest period of the reign on internal evidence, since the invader is nowhere mentioned and the king is friendly with Egypt, and explains the arrangement by the compiler's principle, these narratives being brought together because each turns on the conflict with the false prophets. Keil and Delitzsch note the chapter's own heading and reject a proposal that the chapters following form three supplements on true and false prophethood, since Micah was far from a false prophet and Urijah as little wanting in courage as the man who himself hid from this king. Calvin concludes that the book was not put together in order but collected.

Whether this is the earlier temple sermon over again divides them quietly. Ellicott reports the critics who take the fuller discourse for the text and this for an epitome, and finds confirmation in the reception, since the surprise and anger that met the mention of Shiloh suggest it was heard now for the first time. Calvin allows that the prophet spoke more at large and thought it enough to show in few words what had been committed to him.

Where he was to stand, and to whom, is deliberate. Gill takes the court for the great court where the people met, and Ellicott supposes a feast, which drew worshippers from every part of the kingdom. Calvin presses the choice of audience: the people could not enter the house itself, so the prophet was placed where all could hear, and though of the priestly order he would have gained little by addressing the Levites. He finds the priests and false prophets passed over on purpose, since none are in so hopeless a case, while a people led astray by them may still be restored.

The order not to diminish a word draws out Henry furthest. He defends the choice of place and time against any charge of indiscretion, since the message might have been delivered in a corner among friends, and the court was the one place within his sworn enemies' jurisdiction, where the worshippers would credit whatever character the priests gave him. He then supplies the reason: the prophet might be tempted to palliate the matter and make it better to his hearers than God had made it to him, exchanging an offensive expression for a plausible one, and God's ambassadors must keep to their instructions and vary neither to please men nor to save themselves from harm. Ellicott adds that there was something in the message from which he would naturally have shrunk.

The tentative phrase about hearkening raises the last question. Gill denies that it expresses ignorance or conjecture in God, taking it for a longsuffering that grants space for repentance and leaves the disregarder without excuse. Calvin agrees it is a common way of speaking and that God had no doubt what would follow, and finds the people's obstinacy the thing pointed at, since it is hard to heal those grown putrid in their evils, and yet he would try. Ellicott puts it as purpose, the terrible threat being uttered in order that it may not be realised. Calvin closes on the pairing of law and prophets, redundant if the law sufficed, and answers that the prophets devised nothing new but were its interpreters, so that those who repudiate the daily duty of learning extinguish the grace of the Spirit.
7:
That the crowd let him finish is read three ways. Henry allows them the credit, since they let him say all he had to say, which is more than some persecutors of ministers have done, though he suspects a bad design, a hope of hearing something worse to lay to his charge. Gill offers two motives, reverence for a man who was both priest and prophet, or a secret influence that kept them from disturbing him. Calvin refuses the credit: there was no teachable spirit in them, and what looks like patience is the feigned moderation of hypocrites, exact beyond need in what is formal and negligent of what is important, who restrained themselves only because the whole people stood by.

The prophets among the accusers are the sharper thing. Gill reports that the older versions call them false prophets. Calvin finds nothing strange in the priests keeping a hereditary title, but marks the other word as strange, and explains that the prophet allows an honourable name to men who boasted they were sent from above while esteeming it as nothing. Ellicott makes it personal, since the accused had to separate himself from both orders he belonged to, the one by birth and the other by a special vocation, his bitterest foes being men who claimed to speak in the same name while tuning their voice to the time. Wesley states it as a rule, that in the corrupt state of all kingdoms the ecclesiastical officers have always been the greatest enemies of God's ministers.

The charge itself is examined. Gill puts the offence in the use of the name, since in his own the words would have passed. Henry shows the misquotation: the threat had been conditional and had God for its agent, and the accusers drop both to leave a flat prediction against the holy place, the same charge afterwards laid against Christ and Stephen. Calvin grants their premise some weight, since a promise of perpetual habitation and a sentence of desolation seem to make God contrary to himself, and answers that the promise was never given as a licence to sin. Ellicott finds the offence in the comparison, since they had exulted over the fall of the northern sanctuary and chanted the psalm that told how God forsook it, and could not bear the same fate impending on their own house.

Two voices work the legal language. Ellicott renders the sentence with the Hebrew reduplication, thou shalt die the death, and calls the accusers' formula one in current forensic use, a judgment of death for this man; personal rancour, he adds, mingles with the class feeling of a priesthood appealing to the secular arm against a blasphemer. Keil and Delitzsch read the words as a formal sentence and explain the appeal to what the bystanders had heard: the princes reached the temple only after the arrest, so the crowd had to supply the evidence.

Who the princes were is variously answered. Clarke calls them the king's cabinet counsellors, Gill the nobles of the privy council or the great court of seventy; Wesley says the entry where they sat was where the body that judged false prophets used to sit. Ellicott reconstructs the movement, the report reaching them in council with the king and bringing them down by the king's own entry, a high gate commanding the crowded court, and observes that one was in all probability the man who afterwards saved the prophet, the princes throughout being less hostile than the priests. Calvin turns their arrival into a rebuke, since the king sent them only to quell a commotion and none had thought the preaching worth attending, though men had come from remote cities for it. He adds a note on the crowd, like the sea, calm of itself until a wind rises, easily stirred and as easily brought back.
12:
The defence is short, and its shortness is remarked on. Calvin observes that the prophet pleads nothing but his calling and the command he had received, and thinks he might have spoken at large but judged a long discourse would obscure the main point. Ellicott makes it the standing answer of every true prophet, that the Lord has spoken and he can but prophesy, and notes what is absent: the man has no credentials beyond the message itself, having worked no signs or wonders. Clarke gives it in the first person, the commission being God's and the words his own, and he neither sought this painful office nor ran before he was sent. Gill records an old judgment that the plea was made with prudence, humility and constancy.

The plea then repeats the sermon. Ellicott points out that this is the whole apology: no irreversible doom had been denounced, pardon on repentance had been held out, and the threat uttered to produce the repentance that would cancel it. Calvin turns the repetition into a charge of ingratitude, since nothing could be kinder than a call to repent that they might find mercy, and asks what madness it is to be unable to bear that God would forgive them.

The prophet then puts himself in their power, and the phrase is weighed. Gill takes it at face value, since they were the court to which the judging of prophets belonged, and he submits. Ellicott has him powerless before accusers and judges, with no appeal left but to the Judge of all. Clarke keeps the two halves together, do with me what you please, but if you slay me you bring innocent blood upon yourselves. Calvin denies that the words can be read strictly, since a man in his enemies' hand is not out of God's, and tyrants cannot touch us with a finger unless permission is given; the prophet speaks after a human manner and by concession, because providence is hidden and we see only as far as our eyes reach.

The warning about innocent blood is an appeal to particular hearers. Ellicott notes that it is addressed to the lay judges and the people rather than the accusers, on the belief that they at least would shrink from such a deed, and that the protest is one of constraint, a necessity laid on the speaker rather than a wilful attack on what his countrymen revered. Calvin reads the preposition as spreading the guilt two ways, upon the killers as perpetrators and against the city for allowing and countenancing the deed; the warning, he adds, was given not to save the prophet's life but to move them, since he did not fear death and knew his blood would be precious enough to cost the whole city.

The verdict reverses the morning. Gill marks the turn in the crowd, which had sided with the accusers and now joined the court in addressing them. Calvin explains the reversal by the company they were in, since a people blinded by the pomp of the priests would not inquire into the cause and went the other way as soon as the princes were present; he draws from it how mischievous rulers are where there is no regard for justice and how desirable honest ones are, who defend what is right and aid the oppressed. Ellicott finds the later trial coming unbidden to mind, the lay rulers favouring the prophet whom priests would have condemned, save that here the people are on his side. Henry presses the acquittal until it accuses the acquitters: if they own that the man spoke in the name of the Lord, and that this Lord is their God, it is a pity they did not then amend their ways, for men often protect preaching from the malice of others without submitting to its power themselves.
17:
Who the elders were, and when, is not settled. Gill identifies them with the princes, court men rising as advocates. Ellicott prefers the literal sense over the official, or the official including the literal, since the speech requires men old enough to carry the tradition of a century before, and notes that the word rendered assembly answers to the term for a Greek town's citizen body. Clarke calls the defence fine and the argument perfectly conclusive, and reports the guess that it was Ahikam who made it. Calvin doubts the placing, since Scripture does not always keep the order of events, and thinks it likelier that the elders interposed while the case was still under deliberation and the crowd not yet pacified.

The precedent is agreed, its force variously stated. Calvin puts the argument against the charge of novelty: the accused was not the first herald of such a vengeance, God having been wont before this to speak by his prophets against the city and the temple. Clarke draws the comparison, that the earlier prophet said things as hard and was not put to death, the people seeing he was sent of God. Ellicott sharpens it into a principle: here was a case in which a threat did its work and therefore was not fulfilled, doing good and not evil. Gill spells out the negative, that neither the king nor the great court ever sought that prophet's life, sat in council on it, or so much as arraigned him.

The identification occupies three voices. Gill gives the birthplace and concludes from the quotation that this is the prophet whose book stands among the minor prophets. Wesley agrees and paraphrases it, that Zion should be plowed up and the temple's place become so desolate that trees would grow there as in a forest. Ellicott adds the philology, that the Hebrew gives the longer form of the name, the two being interchangeable, and places the birthplace in Philistine territory; since that ministry began two reigns earlier, the words cited must belong near its close, and they stand immediately before a promise of restoration in the last days that appears in identical terms in another book.

What Hezekiah did with the threat is read two ways. Ellicott admits that no record of the repentance survives, holds it in keeping with the king's known character, and hears in the elders' tone the voice of old experience rising almost to prophetic strain, the closing warning answering exactly to a later counsel about being found to fight against God; the result is left to be inferred, and evidently left the prophet free to preach on, though probably under something like surveillance. Calvin defines the fear of the Lord as true conversion, the reverence by which a man shows himself submissive because God is at once Father and Sovereign, and finds repentance in two parts, displeasure with oneself and the desire to form the whole life by the rule of righteousness; the singular verb, he thinks, is used designedly to commend a king of almost incomparable piety.

Calvin alone turns the date into a difficulty, then a comfort. It might seem strange that under so religious a king, who spared no labour and shunned no danger where religion required it, things stood disordered enough to call for so severe a denunciation; but the lesson is that even the chief exemplar of a godly ruler could not make the whole people follow him, and what then must happen where those who ought to show the way are slothful. The good men hearing it were confirmed, since it is a grievous trial to think one's efforts vain, and many go backward. Keil and Delitzsch mark the turn that follows, that the story to come showing the hostility of the king where this one has shown that of the priests and false prophets.
20:
Whose mouth the story of Urijah comes from is disputed. Gill denies that the elders continue speaking, the instance telling against them, and gives it to others in the court who sided with the accusers, asking why an old reign should be cited when there is so recent a case in this one; he cites two Jewish commentators and an ancient book, while allowing that some take it for the defenders arguing that a second such death would add sin to sin. Calvin canvasses both, notes that the connecting particle may be read adversatively, and comes down for the defenders, moved by the common consent of interpreters and by the two examples running on with nothing between, so the accusers must already have had their turn. Ellicott takes neither side, holding that the verses cannot belong to the elders' argument, telling as they do the other way, and that nothing says the accusers alleged them; the narrator, he thinks, wished to record that this prophet did not stand alone, one man having been faithful found among the faithless.

Why the second man fared differently is asked by two. Ellicott finds it suggestive that the princes who defended one were against the other, and offers a choice, that his words were more vehemently denunciatory or that he was less fortunate in finding a protector. Calvin uses the flight to concede that even faithful servants of God are not always courageous enough to despise every danger; the fear was not blameless, but did not turn the man from his course, for he might have pleased the king and dreaded such perfidy more than death.

The pursuit is filled in politically. Ellicott recalls that the king owed his throne to Egypt, and identifies the envoy as his father-in-law, whose own father had worked with Shaphan in the reformation, and who appears later among the princes friendly to the prophet. Calvin makes the recovery diplomacy rather than force, since the king complained of a turbulent fugitive and asked for his surrender, so the man was brought back by a nefarious compact and not by any power reaching into Egypt.

The burial draws the strongest language. Ellicott calls it brutal outrage by Jewish feeling, the body denied the sepulchre of its fathers and the honour of embalmment and flung into the loathsome pits of the common people; and he notes, for those who believe in a special as well as a righteous retribution, that the king who added this brutality to his cruelty was himself afterwards buried with the burial of an ass. Calvin explains the practice, the rich being buried honourably and each having his own grave, while a great number are thrown together because it would cost too much to dig for each; the wrath burned so hot that a fresh disgrace was prepared for the prophet after death.

How the accused escaped comes last. Keil and Delitzsch close the narrative on the reason, that one man's hand was with him, and identify him among those Josiah had sent to consult the prophetess. Ellicott makes the family the point, three generations of patriotism: the father superintended the restoration of the house, received the recovered book of the law and carried it to the king, and took this son with him to the prophetess; the son now protects the prophet whose work rested so largely on that book's impression, and the grandson later shelters him as governor. Gill and Wesley make the protector one of the old king's counsellors, who used all his power and interest. Clarke adds the danger that remained, since acquittal did not remove the popular prejudice and the man was likely obliged to conceal him, God's genuine ministers having no favour to expect from his enemies. Calvin reads the adversative particle as the measure of the struggle, hand in Scripture meaning effort.
